Voxels are rendered as points to the 64-bit visibility buffer [S1].

The claim states that 'Voxels are rendered as points to the 64-bit visibility buffer'. Section 2.3 of the source text explicitly states: 'For each frame, the voxels are rendered as points to a 64-bit visibility buffer [Burns and Hunt 2013].' This matches the claim exactly.
supported
The renderer reconstructs voxels from the visibility buffer using a method similar to Nanite [Karis et al. 2021] [S1].

The source text explicitly states in Section 2.3 'Render a Frame': 'Then in the next pass, the renderer reconstructs the voxel from the visibility buffer. Differing from the last pass, we use a method similar to Nanite [Karis et al. 2021] to render voxels.' This directly supports the claim.
supported
Frustum culling is applied to cull any invisible cells before rendering [S1].

The claim states that frustum culling is applied to cull invisible cells before rendering. Source [S1], specifically in Section 2.3 'Render a Frame', explicitly states: 'When rendering each cell, frustum culling is used to cull any invisible cells.' This directly supports the claim.

The claim states that the average frame time was 6.0459 ms at 4K resolution on a Windows 10 desktop with AMD Threadripper 2950X and RTX4090, measured during a camera fly-through of a 16x16 chunk test scene (4^12 resolution). Source [S1] explicitly confirms all these details in Section 3 ('RESULT AND CONCLUSION'): 'The example renderer runs on a Windows 10 desktop with AMD Threadripper 2950X and RTX4090. The average frame time is 6.0459 ms under 4K resolution and the result is measured by the camera fly-through of the test scene.' It also confirms the scene details: 'Our test scene contains 16x16 chunks... Therefore, the resolution of this test scene is 4^12.' All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.

1.  **STree (Streaming Tree):** A low-level sparse octree contained within chunks of a high-level 2D uniform grid [S1].

The claim states that STree is a low-level sparse octree contained within chunks of a high-level 2D uniform grid. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in Section 2.1: 'VirtualVoxel scenes employ a two-level structure for streaming voxel data. The high-level structure consists of a 2D uniform grid, with each grid chunk containing a low-level sparse octree. We refer to this Octree as the STree...'

If $LOD\_error \le 0$ or the cell is a leaf node, a cell-building request is sent to the GPU [S1].

The claim states that if LOD_error <= 0 or the cell is a leaf node, a cell-building request is sent to the GPU. Source [S1] explicitly states in Section 2.2 Streaming: 'Whenever a suitable LOD is found or this cell is a leaf node, a cell-building request is sent to GPU.' The notes clarify that a 'suitable LOD' corresponds to LOD_error <= 0 (since if LOD_error > 0, child cells are evaluated). Thus, the evidence fully supports the claim.

It streams appropriate levels of detail into GPU memory using a two-level data structure, storing data linearly to enable efficient real-time scene editing (Union/Subtraction) [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that VirtualVoxel uses a 'two-level structure' (high-level 2D uniform grid and low-level sparse octree/STree) to stream appropriate levels of detail into GPU memory. It confirms that data is stored 'linearly' (unlike graph-based methods) and that this approach enables 'efficient modification' of large scenes, specifically supporting 'Union and Subtraction' operations for real-time editing.

During voxelization, voxels residing within subtraction cubes are eliminated [S1].

The claim states that during voxelization, voxels residing within subtraction cubes are eliminated. Source [S1], specifically in Section 2.4 'Real-Time Modification', explicitly states: 'During voxelization, the voxelizer eliminates voxels from cells by verifying whether a voxel resides within the subtraction cube.' This directly supports the claim.
supported
*   **Storage:** Only existence flags are recorded for each cell to allow efficient storage and access of sparse data [S1].

The claim states that 'Only existence flags are recorded for each cell to allow efficient storage and access of sparse data'. This is directly supported by the text in Section 2.2 Streaming, which states: 'For each cell of STree, we only record whether it exists, allowing us to efficiently store and access sparse voxel data.' The phrase 'record whether it exists' corresponds to recording 'existence flags', and the purpose 'efficiently store and access sparse voxel data' matches the claim's purpose.
supported
If $LOD\_error > 0$, the CPU evaluates child cells, as the current cell does not meet the LOD metric [S1].

The claim states that if LOD_error > 0, the CPU evaluates child cells because the current cell does not meet the LOD metric. This is explicitly confirmed in Source [S1], Section 2.2 Streaming, which states: 'If the LOD error is above zero, the CPU evaluates the child cells, as the current cell does not meet the LOD metric.'
